title: Prefix-aware shape hedging and JIT kernel routing - runtime proposal
content:
Purpose:

This is a working proposal for a lightweight runtime layer that: (1) reduces wasted compute due to over-padding, (2) keeps KV cache semantics correct for served chat-style workloads, and (3) enables JIT kernel switching based on compacted shapes. The aim is an incremental change we can A/B and roll out on dedicated pools before enabling on hosted.

Background / motivation:

We routinely see tail latency and cost inflation from naive padding when requests vary from 8 tokens to 1,024 tokens. Existing approaches (strict length-based buckets, static packers) either over-partition traffic or suffer from fragmentation when users do many short interactive prompts layered on top of long contexts. Additionally, switching between kernels (e.g., FlashAttention vs tiled attention, quantized vs fp16) is brittle when the runtime does not have a predictable shape. KV cache complicates matters: compaction / trimming techniques must preserve positional keys and cache index mapping for resumed decoding.

Goals and non-goals:

Goals:
- Reduce average padded token work per request by 20–40% for mixed-length workloads without increasing tail latency beyond 5%.
- Maintain exact KV cache semantics for resumed chat continuations (no staleness or misalignment).
- Support safe JIT kernel selection per micro-batch with simple rollback/fallback rules.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not propose a new model format or tokenizer behavior.
- Not targeting full rework of scheduler; we expect to extend existing time/size hybrid scheduler.

Design overview (high level):

Introduce a thin runtime layer called "shape hedging" that sits between request admission and the packer. Shape hedging performs a fast heuristic analysis of input tokens and existing KV metadata and computes a compacted execution shape and a set of constraints that downstream stages must honour. Main components:

1) Prefix-aware compaction ruleset (compaction layer)
- Left-trim compaction: when a request contains a long system or instruction prefix followed by a short user turn, allow left-trim (clip earliest repeated contiguous prefix embeddings) for execution packing only if the request indicates the prefix is immutable and KV offsets can be adjusted. We will tag compaction allowed only when the request includes a stable conversation id and an explicit resume flag.
- Suffix-only trimming: for generation-initiated truncation we support controlled suffix truncation where the first N tokens of the history are collapsed into a single pseudo-token representation that preserves token count metadata for position indices.
- Hash-stable prefix dedupe: identical prefixes across concurrent requests in a micro-batch can be deduplicated into one cached context vector; we materialize per-request position delta metadata to reconstruct outputs.

2) Shape cohorts and micro-batches (scheduler)
- Instead of strict length buckets, we form short-lived "shape cohorts" (e.g., {<=32, 33-96, 97-256, 257-1024}) but allow dynamic cohort merging when arrival patterns yield a dominant centroid. Cohort formation is probabilistic and computed every scheduling tick (5–20ms).
- Hybrid time/size microbatching remains: we schedule on a target token-work cap, but prefer cohort-aligned packing to avoid intra-batch padding explosion.
- When compaction rules create per-request position offsets, the scheduler records mapping metadata that the runtime uses for KV slice lookups and output decompaction.

3) JIT kernel routing (kernel selection)
- Kernel selection is done at micro-batch time using a deterministic heuristic: estimate memory working set (batch_size * compacted_seq_len * model_unit), check quantization compatibility, and pick preferred kernels ordered by: FlashAttention-optimized -> Tiled-attn -> Compatibility fallback (slower fused kernels).
- We keep a fast cost model (simple arithmetic) rather than a heavy profiler in the hot path; the cost model is periodically calibrated offline.
- Kernel switch includes a safety check: if chosen kernel lacks an optimized KV recomposition path for per-request offsets, we either (a) use a compatible kernel or (b) materialize full KV (no compaction) as fallback.

4) KV cache handling and mapping (KV layer)
- Per-request metadata: when compaction applies, we attach offset_map: a small vector (start_pos, compacted_length, original_length) as stringified metadata. This is carried through scheduling and used to map attention positions back to original indices when writing/reading the global KV store.
- Partial KV slices: store and fetch KV in variable-length slices keyed by (request_id, compacted_pos_range). The global KV store remains authoritative but accepts compacted slices and materializes missing ranges lazily when a compaction-aware miss occurs.
- Eviction semantics: keep TTL-based eviction plus LRU by compacted-size; eviction logs include decompaction hints to allow fast re-materialization.

Dataflow example (chat resume):
- Client resumes conversation C, sending last 3 turns with a long immutable system prompt.
- Shape hedging detects stable system prefix and marks it for prefix dedupe; compacted_length drops by ~60% for the micro-batch.
- Scheduler assigns cohort <=96, picks FlashAttention kernel; kernel supports offset-aware KV lookup.
- Execution uses compacted KV slices; after generation results are decompacted using recorded offset_map so token positions align with original conversation history.

Fallback and safety rules:
- If any request in the micro-batch has KV constraints that cannot be represented (e.g., unaligned positional embeddings due to custom position shifting), we fallback to conservative packer (no compaction) for entire micro-batch.
- Latency SLO guard: if micro-batch compaction path adds >10ms overhead in scheduling, disable compaction for that shard for 1 minute.

Metrics to collect / experiments:
- Delta padded tokens per micro-batch (baseline vs compaction).
- Tail latency (95/99) and p50 with compaction enabled.
- KV miss rate and re-materialization time.
- Kernel switch correctness test coverage: logits equivalence within epsilon for selected kernels when compaction is active.
- Cost model accuracy: predicted vs measured GPU memory and time.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How much complexity are we willing to accept in the global KV store? Partial slices help cost but increase implementation surface.
- Deduplication correctness: do we need stronger semantic markers from the client (e.g., "system_immutable") or can heuristics be sufficient?
- Quantization interplay: some quantized kernels do not support fine-grained KV slice offsets; fallback policies must be cheap.

Implementation plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (spike): implement simulator and offline trace replay to measure potential savings on historical production traffic (2 weeks).
- Phase 1 (infrastructure): add offset_map metadata plumbing and minimal KV slice APIs; add cohort-aware scheduler hooks (4–6 weeks).
- Phase 2 (eng): implement compaction heuristics and kernel cost model; local unit tests and microbenchmarks (4 weeks).
- Phase 3 (canary): enable on dedicated pool with canary traffic, collect metrics, iterate (4 weeks).

Next steps / action items:
- Evan: set up trace replay harness and produce an initial savings estimate by 2024-10-25.
- Priya: prototype offset_map wire format and KV slice API spec (doc) by 2024-11-01.
- Diego: add microbenchmark to kernel bench repo for offset-aware FlashAttention behavior by 2024-11-08.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative on semantic guarantees: we preserve exact position mapping always, even when compaction is in play. The tradeoff is small metadata overhead for large CPU wins.
- We should keep the user-visible debugging artifact: a decompacted token map that can be returned in debug mode to verify alignment.

Unresolved:
- Exact compacted metadata encoding size targets (we should cap offset_map to <=64 bytes per request to avoid network blowup).
- Formal verification plan for compaction + KV interactions (ideas: small model reference tests + fuzzing).
